Well the main reasons are pretty much the same as the ones to get a better car, but these benefits come from 5-100 dollars rather than 5,000-40,000. First of all, the feel of the pen while writing is much different. With a ballpoint you will have to press down hard to write at all, causing your hand to become strained and your handwriting to be less neat. Modern gel and rollerball pens solve some of these problems, but a fountain will still require the least amount of pressure. With a finely tuned pen you might not even need to press down at all, and the pen will not have friction going across the page. Some people want the friction on the page so they have more control, so another nice thing about fountain pens is that you can control that and change the smoothness and wetness to your desire (but it may require micromesh). At the same time you can choose how wide you want your pen to write, or you could do calligraphy with a stub or italic nib or even flex some nibs for a different type of calligraphy. Not only do you choose the size of the writing, you can choose from almost unlimited colors, and inks that have different properties like water resistance, pigments such as chlorophyll(the maker of this ink stopped making that ink though so very little is left), scents, and even the ability to glow in the dark. The materials are also not just cheap plastic, if you name a material it has probably been made into a pen before or could be - even cheese plastic you could make at home and eat (paneer/casein). The materials have different colors or may feel differently in the hand like something other than lifeless plastic, as well as having some heft. The ways to refill the pen are also more interesting; some have a piston inside the pen that you work by twisting the back, some have a mini and removable version that fits inside the barrel, some have little plastic tubes that attach to the pen, some even absorb ink with magic (coated in teflon)!. Another allure of fountain pens (and nice pens) is the feel that you have a pen made to last, and one that could outlast you at that (I own a pen from the 20's/30's), or the patronage of an artist.
Have you ever wondered if you should get a little nicer pen? or maybe even just a low-price fountain pen?

Not being in any of the mentioned industries, I can't give you an inside scoop, but I can tell you that the way you'd go about becoming a piano repair technician is probably going to be wildly different than becoming a welder. However, here's some things I found that might be helpful to you if you're seriously thinking about welding or instrument repair. (I'm assuming you're an American. If you aren't, well, I guess I'll have to amend some information here.)

Welding

  • Most places I've seen suggest if you're in high school, taking every class you can that includes welding in it. Companies hiring welding positions are really keen on seeing that a kid fresh out of high school have spent time already learning how to weld.

  • Post-high school? Several employers are just looking for anyone who can hold a welder, and work hard, so previous experience isn't necessarily a must if they're willing to train you. Looking for a company that has training (bonus for paid training!) might not be the easiest way into the industry (there will be more competition for the position) but if you have a clear work history of hard work, it's possible to make it into a welding position that will teach you all you need to know, and possibly lead to a career. Take note though, you'll still need to become a Certified Welder credited by the American Welding Society. This would just be a way to break into the industry.

  • Several unions are also willing to train you, so looking into a union might be worth it to you.

  • You can go to a technical school to get a welding degree to break into the industry. Here's a website that's a pretty good resource for finding a good technical college you might be interested in. Additionally, the American Welding Society has resources for finding education you'll need to make welding a viable career. I suggest you take some time perusing their website because it's pretty good about providing links for further research into any given topic. Instrument Repair

  • The first thing that I read, and the thing that stuck the most with me as a good bit of common sense is that if you're going to repair an instrument, it helps to know how to play it. If you know how to play many different instruments, it will help.

  • I didn't find as much about instrument repair as I did welding (it turns out, it's not as popular, go figure) but I did find the National Association of Professional Band Instrument Repair Technicians website, which like the AWS website, lists some places to become educated to work in the field.

  • [Here's an article] on a website devoted to careers in music which mentions woodworking or metalworking also being a requirement for being a repair technician, which you should keep in mind when considering whether you'd rather go into welding or instrument repair.

  • I actually found a youtube video where a technician talks about his career in repairing instruments, if you're interested.

So that's about as much as I was able to find. I hope it was at least a little helpful. Both welding and instrument repair can potentially be very good sources of income, but both need some extra schooling beforehand. In both cases, there's technical colleges you can attend, which will cost you less than a traditional 4 year college, but it will still take a bit of time and money.
